title: Principles of Tooth Preparation II — Test

mcqs.q: Retention form is the quality of a preparation that prevents dislodgment by forces directed:
opts: Parallel to the path of placement
In an apical or oblique direction
mcqs.explain: Retention resists removal along (parallel to) the path of placement; resistance opposes apical/oblique forces and movement under occlusal load.

mcqs.q: Resistance form is the quality that prevents dislodgment by forces directed:
opts: In an apical or oblique direction
Parallel to the path of placement
mcqs.explain: Resistance prevents dislodgment by apical/oblique forces and any movement of the restoration under occlusal forces.

mcqs.q: The ideal total occlusal convergence (taper) of the axial walls is approximately:
mcqs.explain: A taper of ~6° is the practical ideal; more taper reduces retention, while truly parallel walls are clinically difficult and risk undercuts.

mcqs.q: As the taper of the axial walls increases, retention:
mcqs.explain: Even a small increase in axial-wall taper significantly reduces retention (more tapered walls → less retention).

mcqs.q: Which preparation is MOST retentive?
opts: A molar full crown with tall axial walls
A premolar full crown with short walls
A crown on a preparation with an undercut
mcqs.explain: Retention increases with taller walls, greater diameter (molars > premolars) and full > partial coverage; undercuts prevent seating.

mcqs.q: Adding grooves or boxes to a preparation improves retention and resistance by:
opts: Limiting the number of paths of withdrawal
mcqs.explain: Grooves/boxes restrict the paths along which the restoration can be withdrawn, increasing both retention and resistance.

mcqs.q: Line angles of a preparation should be rounded, especially occluso-axial ones, in order to:
opts: Minimise stress concentration and cement failure
mcqs.explain: Sharp line angles concentrate stress, causing cohesive failure of the luting cement and loss of retention; rounding them minimises stress.

mcqs.q: Using conventional luting cement, retention by the cemented material is generally greatest with:
mcqs.explain: With conventional cement, retention order is base-metal alloy > gold alloy > ceramic.

mcqs.q: Which luting agent generally provides the greatest retention?
mcqs.explain: Retention by luting agent: resin > GIC > zinc phosphate ≈ zinc polycarboxylate > ZnO-eugenol.

mcqs.q: The ideal film thickness of the luting agent is:
mcqs.explain: An ideal cement film thickness is about 20–25 µm, allowing complete seating with adequate retention.

mcqs.q: Resistance form is a function of the relationship between taper, diameter and height. Which change INCREASES resistance?
mcqs.explain: ↑height → ↑resistance; ↑taper → ↓resistance; ↑diameter → ↓resistance; grooves/boxes and full coverage increase resistance.

mcqs.q: A patient who bruxes or smokes a pipe is relevant to resistance form because such habits:
opts: Apply large oblique forces to the restoration
mcqs.explain: Habits like bruxism or pipe smoking apply large oblique/horizontal forces that a preparation's resistance form must withstand.

mcqs.q: To prevent deformation, the recommended minimum alloy thickness over a FUNCTIONAL cusp is about:
mcqs.explain: ≈1.5 mm over functional cusps and 1 mm over non-functional cusps provides adequate strength against deformation.

mcqs.q: Regarding occlusal preparation, which statement is correct?
opts: The amount of clearance is more significant than the amount of reduction
Reduction always matters more than clearance
Clearance is irrelevant for supra-erupted teeth
mcqs.explain: Adequate clearance (space for material) is more significant than the raw amount of reduction; favour preparations with no acute/sharp angles.

mcqs.q: Inadequate axial reduction typically results in:
opts: Thin weak walls or a bulbous, overcontoured restoration
mcqs.explain: Too little axial reduction forces either thin, weak restoration walls or an over-contoured, bulbous crown.

mcqs.q: Which restoration best mimics natural tooth colour but is LEAST conservative of tooth structure?
mcqs.explain: All-ceramic restorations reproduce colour best but need generous reduction and a specific finish line, so they are not conservative.

mcqs.q: For a metal-ceramic crown, the minimum facial reduction for optimal appearance is about:
mcqs.explain: A minimum facial reduction of ~1.5 mm is needed for adequate porcelain thickness and appearance.

mcqs.q: The labial/facial surface of an anterior metal-ceramic preparation should be prepared in:
mcqs.explain: Preparing in two planes avoids under-reduction of either the cervical or incisal area, which a single plane would cause.

mcqs.q: The recommended incisal reduction for a metal-ceramic restoration is about:
mcqs.explain: About 2 mm incisal reduction gives good esthetics; excessive incisal reduction reduces resistance and retention.

mcqs.q: Anterior proximal surfaces look most natural when restored so that:
opts: The incisal proximal areas are porcelain without metal backing
The whole proximal surface is metal
A thick metal collar is placed labially
mcqs.explain: Restoring proximal areas in porcelain without metal backing lets light pass through like a natural tooth; FDP connectors make this impossible. Light passes through.

mcqs.q: When placing a subgingival labial margin for esthetics, which is TRUE?
opts: The periodontium must be healthy before preparation
The margin may extend to the alveolar crest
Thin gingiva hides a metal collar best
mcqs.explain: Subgingival margins require a healthy periodontium; the margin follows the free-gingival contour, and extension to within 1.5 mm of the alveolar crest causes bone resorption.

mcqs.q: A subgingival margin should NOT be placed closer to the alveolar crest than:
mcqs.explain: Encroaching within 1.5 mm of the alveolar crest violates the attachment and leads to bone resorption.

mcqs.q: Partial-coverage restorations are preferred when possible mainly because:
opts: Tooth structure is conserved and intact enamel looks best
They are always stronger than full crowns
They are more retentive than full crowns
mcqs.explain: Partial coverage conserves tooth structure and no material matches intact enamel; esthetics depend on accurate facial/proximal margin placement.

mcqs.q: The facial margin of a partial cast crown should be shaped so that:
opts: Light is not reflected directly to the observer
It sits on the incisal edge
It is placed on the contact point
mcqs.explain: Correct facial-margin contouring prevents direct light reflection to the observer, keeping the metal esthetically acceptable.

mcqs.q: Diagnostic tooth preparations performed on articulated casts help to determine all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: The path of placement for an FDP with tilted abutments
The amount of reduction for a planned occlusal change
The best location of facial/proximal margins so metal is hidden
mcqs.explain: Diagnostic preparations reveal path of placement, needed reduction and margin location; caries risk is a diagnostic (not a wax-up) matter.

mcqs.q: During preparation, holding the top surface of the handpiece parallel to the occlusal surface ensures:
opts: Correct axial alignment of the rotary instrument
mcqs.explain: Keeping the handpiece's top surface parallel to the occlusal surface keeps the bur in correct axial alignment, establishing the intended convergence.

mcqs.q: The correct convergence of the axial walls is established clinically by:
opts: Moving the tapered diamond parallel to itself around the tooth
Using a round bur perpendicular to the axis
Preparing each wall at a random angle
mcqs.explain: Moving the tapered diamond parallel to itself around the tooth reproduces the diamond's taper as a uniform, controlled convergence.

mcqs.q: The magnitude of the dislodging force acting on a restoration depends largely on:
opts: The stickiness of the food and the surface area and texture of the restoration being pulled
The thickness of the luting agent alone
mcqs.explain: The more retentive the preparation, the better it resists these forces.

mcqs.q: Which preparation geometry gives the GREATEST retention?
opts: Tall axial walls of large diameter — a molar rather than a premolar
Short axial walls of large diameter
Tall axial walls of small diameter
Short axial walls of small diameter
mcqs.explain: Note the contrast with resistance, where an increase in diameter DECREASES resistance.

mcqs.q: The roughness of the fitting surface affects retention because:
opts: Metal, etchable ceramic and crystalline ceramic differ in bondable roughness
A rougher surface always reduces the film thickness
Roughness removes the need for a luting agent
Smooth surfaces bond better than rough ones in every case
mcqs.explain: This is factor C of the six factors influencing retention.

mcqs.q: All-ceramic restorations mimic natural tooth colour best, but:
opts: NOT conservative — they need generous reduction and a specific finish line
They cannot be used on anterior teeth at all
They always require a metal substructure beneath
They give the greatest retention of any restoration
mcqs.explain: This is the trade-off against their superior esthetics.

mcqs.q: Partial-coverage restorations are preferred whenever possible because:
opts: Tooth structure is conserved and no material matches intact enamel
They are stronger than complete crowns
They are more retentive than complete crowns
mcqs.explain: Their esthetics depend on accurate placement of the visible facial and proximal margins, the facial margin being shaped so light is not reflected directly to the observer.

mcqs.q: During preparation, axial alignment is checked:
opts: Continuously, by direct vision and with the mirror
Only after the preparation is complete
Only on the articulated diagnostic cast
mcqs.explain: The correct convergence is established by moving the tapered diamond parallel to itself around the tooth.

saqs.q: Define retention and resistance form, and list the factors affecting retention.
saqs.a: RETENTION FORM resists dislodgment by forces PARALLEL to the path of placement. RESISTANCE FORM resists forces directed APICALLY or OBLIQUELY and prevents movement under occlusal load. Factors: magnitude of dislodging forces · geometry (taper ~6°, surface area, type of preparation, grooves/boxes, rounded line angles) · roughness of the fitting surface · material cemented (base-metal > gold > ceramic) · luting agent (resin > GIC > zinc phosphate ≈ polycarboxylate > ZOE) · film thickness 20–25 µm.

head: RETENTION form
RESISTANCE form
rows: prevents dislodgment by forces parallel to the path of placement
prevents dislodgment by forces directed apically or obliquely, and prevents movement under occlusal forces
axial-wall taper ~6° · surface area (height and diameter) · type of preparation (full > partial) · grooves and boxes · rounded line angles to reduce stress concentration

saqs.q: How does the geometry of the preparation influence resistance form?
saqs.a: Resistance is a function of taper, diameter and height: increasing TAPER decreases it; increasing DIAMETER decreases it; increasing HEIGHT increases it; grooves and boxes increase it; full coverage beats partial. The magnitude and direction of dislodging forces (bruxism, pipe smoking) and the physical properties of the luting agent also matter.

ans.text: The magnitude and direction of the dislodging forces — e.g. large oblique forces from bruxism or pipe smoking — and the physical properties of the luting agent also matter.

saqs.q: Explain how a restoration is protected against deformation during tooth preparation.
saqs.a: The restoration needs enough strength to resist permanent deformation: a minimum alloy thickness of ~1.5 mm over FUNCTIONAL cusps and 1 mm over NON-FUNCTIONAL cusps. CLEARANCE (occlusal space for the material) matters more than the amount of reduction, and preparations should have no acute or sharp angles. Inadequate axial reduction gives either thin weak walls or a bulbous overcontoured restoration.

list: Clearance — the occlusal space for the material — is more significant than the amount of reduction
Preparations should be favourable, with no acute or sharp angles
Inadequate axial reduction gives either thin, weak walls or a bulbous, overcontoured restoration

saqs.q: Describe the esthetic considerations for metal-ceramic restorations (facial, incisal, proximal reduction and margin placement).
saqs.a: Compromised appearance usually comes from insufficient porcelain thickness. FACIAL — minimum 1.5 mm in TWO planes so neither cervical nor incisal is under-reduced. INCISAL — about 2 mm, avoiding excess which cuts resistance/retention. PROXIMAL — anterior proximals look most natural in porcelain at the incisal edges without metal backing, so light passes through. LABIAL MARGIN — subgingival for a high lip line; the periodontium must be healthy, the margin follows the free-gingival contour and must not lie within 1.5 mm of the alveolar crest.

ans.text: A compromised appearance is usually caused by insufficient porcelain thickness.

saqs.q: What is the role of diagnostic tooth preparations, diagnostic waxing and evaluative procedures in planning a preparation?
saqs.a: DIAGNOSTIC TOOTH PREPARATIONS on articulated casts help select the path of placement (especially with tilted abutments), decide the reduction needed for a planned occlusal change, and locate facial and proximal margins so metal is not visible. DIAGNOSTIC WAXING previews the planned contours and result. EVALUATIVE PROCEDURES during preparation: move the tapered diamond parallel to itself around the tooth to establish convergence, hold the handpiece top parallel to the occlusal surface for axial alignment, and check continually by direct vision and mirror.

saqs.q: List the six factors that influence the retention of a cemented restoration.
saqs.a: A magnitude of dislodging forces — stickiness of food, surface area and texture. B geometry — parallelism (TOC ~6°), wall height and diameter, type (full coverage > double partial), grooves and boxes. C roughness of the fitting surface. D material cemented — base-metal > gold > ceramic. E luting agent — resin > GIC > zinc phosphate and polycarboxylate > ZOE. F film thickness — ideally 20–25 µm.
